## Q1. Attrition rate for employees at BI:

```{r}
# attrition rate function
attrition_rate <- function(x) {
  mean(x == "Yes")
}
```

### Overall attrition rate

```{r}
# Overall attrition rate
attrition_rate(bioimplant$attrition)
```

### Summary Table

```{r}
# Conditional rates by department and job role
attrition_table <- bioimplant %>%
  group_by(department, job_role) %>%
  summarise(
    attrition_rate = attrition_rate(attrition),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(attrition_rate))

head(attrition_table)
```

## Q2. Logistic regression model of attrition using all predictors:

```{r}
# setting the binomial levels
bioimplant$attrition <- factor(bioimplant$attrition, levels = c("No", "Yes"))

# model using everything but employee_number
log_model <- glm(
  attrition ~ . - employee_number,
  data = bioimplant,
  family = binomial
)

# summary(log_model)

# Predict "Yes" when the predicted probability is at least 0.5
predicted_probability <- predict(log_model, type = "response")
predicted_class <- ifelse(predicted_probability >= 0.5, "Yes", "No")

# comparing predicted category with actual. Result is proportion of correctly classified
accuracy <- mean(predicted_class == as.character(bioimplant$attrition))
cat("Predicted Accuracy:")
accuracy

# Majority class accuracy: predict "No" for every employee
majority_accuracy <- mean(bioimplant$attrition == "No")
cat("Majority Accuracy:")
majority_accuracy
```

### Model vs predicted comparison:

The majority class accuracy os 0.8388 and the predicted accuracy of the model is 0.8925 improving the majority 0.0537 or 5.37 percentage points.

## Q3. Compare Attrition Predictors Using Standardized Logistic Regression Coefficients:

```{r}
# scaling the numeric data
bioimplant_scaled <- bioimplant %>%
  mutate(across(
    where(is.numeric),
    ~ as.numeric(scale(.x))
  ))

# another logistic regression using the scaled data removing employee_number and departmentı
scaled_log_model <- glm(
  attrition ~ . - employee_number,
  data = bioimplant_scaled,
  family = binomial
)

# summary(scaled_log_model)

# Find the largest coefficient by absolute value, excluding the intercept
coefs <- coef(scaled_log_model)
coefs <- coefs[names(coefs) != "(Intercept)"]
coefs[which.max(abs(coefs))]
```


## Q4. Based on the above logistic regression model (and, specifically, on the coefficient with the largest effect size that you identified above), how might company policy be changed to reduce employee attrition?

<!-- Describe your proposed policy change.

Estimate and explain the change in churn probability associated with that policy change. -->

```{r}
p_current <- predict(scaled_log_model, type = "response")

no_overtime <- bioimplant_scaled
no_overtime$over_time <- "No"

p_no_overtime <- predict(
  scaled_log_model,
  newdata = no_overtime,
  type = "response"
)

mean(p_current)
mean(p_no_overtime)
mean(p_no_overtime) - mean(p_current)
```

## Q5. What should Angelica say in her report? Please include quantitative details from your answers to the questions above.

BioImplants’ overall attrition rate is **16.1%** (237 of 1,470 employees). Attrition varies by department and job role: it is highest among Sales Representatives at **39.8%**, followed by Laboratory Technicians at **23.9%** and Human Resources employees in the Human Resources role at **23.1%**.

A logistic regression using the predictors other than employee number correctly classified **89.3%** of employees in this dataset at a 0.5 decision threshold. That is **5.4 percentage points** above the **83.9%** accuracy from predicting “No” attrition for everyone, the majority class. This is in-sample accuracy and should not be treated as evidence of how well the model will predict attrition for new employees.

In the standardized model, refit without department because it overlaps with job role, the largest coefficient was for working overtime (**1.974**, or about **7.2 times the odds** of attrition compared with not working overtime, holding other predictors constant). This suggests reviewing overtime practices—for example, by improving staffing and workload distribution. In a model-based scenario that changes every employee’s overtime status to “No” while holding other predictors fixed, the average predicted attrition probability falls from **16.1% to 10.3%**, a decrease of about **5.9 percentage points**. This is an estimate based on the model’s associations, not proof that reducing overtime would cause attrition to fall by that amount.
